questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a genuine manipulation check in a crew study
questions.stem: A dispatch study tells crews that a revised trip-safety briefing will be evaluated. Which measure is a genuine manipulation check?

options.text: A question confirming that crews actually received and understood the new briefing, kept separate from the outcome.
The count of crews who received the briefing, which proves they read and understood it.
options.misconception: Treats receipt as evidence of understanding.

options.text: Crews' satisfaction with the briefing, which shows whether it changed their practice.
options.misconception: Uses an opinion measure instead of a direct check.

options.text: The number of safety reports filed, which indicates whether crews behaved differently.
options.misconception: Confuses the outcome measure with the manipulation check.

questions.explanation: A manipulation check verifies that the intended change happened for each participant, independently of the outcome. Receipt, satisfaction, and outcome counts answer different questions and cannot substitute for it.
questions.hint: Ask what must be confirmed before the outcome means anything.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise how a post-hoc exclusion distorts a reported average
questions.stem: A log shows the analyst removed the two crews whose results were farthest from the average. What does that do to the reported result?

options.text: It pulls the estimate toward the middle and hides genuine variation, so the rule should have been fixed beforehand.
It makes the estimate more accurate, because outliers are always errors in measurement.
options.misconception: Assumes extreme results are always mistakes.

options.text: It leaves the estimate unchanged, because excluding extremes never moves a mean.
options.misconception: Denies the effect of trimming on a mean.

options.text: It reduces the chance of a false finding, because a smaller spread makes results more reliable.
options.misconception: Treats a smaller spread as evidence of a stronger effect.

questions.explanation: Removing the extremes pulls the average toward the centre and shrinks the spread, which flatters the middle values. Exclusion rules set after seeing the data are what preregistration is meant to prevent.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a one-sided literature search distorts a review's conclusion
questions.stem: A review of automated dispatching systems cites fourteen studies, all of which found benefits, and none of the six published studies reporting neutral or negative results. Explain why this review is misleading.

answer.exemplar: The review has searched only the literature that supports its preferred conclusion, which is publication and selection bias. Studies with neutral or negative findings are more likely to remain unpublished or to be filed away, so the fourteen studies are not a fair sample of the evidence. A credible review states its search terms and databases, includes studies regardless of direction, and explains why any eligible study was excluded.

questions.explanation: Including only supportive studies turns the review into an argument rather than an assessment of the evidence. The missing neutral and negative studies are those most likely to show where the effect fails.
questions.hint: Ask what the review chose not to look at.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a flaw in how a literature search screens and excludes studies

stimulus.body: A reading log lists a search of two dispatch journals for studies on crew fatigue and delay reporting between 2015 and 2024. The log records 31 studies screened, 14 included, and 12 excluded for using a different delay definition. questions.stem: What problem in this reading log does the board need to raise?

options.text: Exclusions were made on titles and abstracts alone, so the recorded reason may not reflect the study's findings.
The search covered only two journals, so it must be repeated in every transport journal in existence.
options.misconception: Demands an impossible standard of coverage.

options.text: The window ends in 2024, so studies before 2015 must be added to make the review complete.
options.misconception: Treats the stated date range as an error.

options.text: Only 14 studies were included, so the search should be abandoned and replaced with a single study.
options.misconception: Treats a modest count as grounds for abandoning.

questions.explanation: Screening on titles and abstracts can exclude studies whose findings differ from what the reviewer expects, which is how a search ends up citing only supportive work. Each exclusion needs a checkable reason.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a post-hoc exclusion removes evidence of the problem
questions.stem: A dispatcher analyst excludes every shift with more than two reported delays, after seeing that shifts with many delays pull the average delay figure up. Explain what this rule does to the evidence.

answer.exemplar: The rule removes the shifts most likely to reveal the problem, so it systematically shrinks the measured delay average and hides the operational strain the agency needs to see. A delay figure produced this way no longer describes the service as experienced. The defensible approach is either to define delay handling in advance, or to report both the full distribution and any exclusion with its reason, so that a reader can see exactly what was removed.

questions.explanation: Excluding the most extreme cases removes evidence of the problem rather than noise, and doing it after seeing results distorts the estimate. Removal needs a pre-set rule and disclosure.
questions.hint: Ask which shifts the rule keeps and which it removes.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a comparison with last year's figures is hard to defend
questions.stem: A planner wants to show that the new dispatch rule cut delays by 30 percent by comparing today's figures with last year's. Explain why that comparison is hard to defend.

answer.exemplar: Last year's figures come from a different network, with different service levels, traffic, staffing, and reporting practice, so a 30 percent improvement may reflect the surrounding conditions rather than the new rule. A defensible comparison uses data from the same routes and the same measurement method, checks that nothing else changed over the period, and preferably adds an unaffected route as a control so that general trends can be separated from the rule's effect.

questions.explanation: A historical baseline differs in service, traffic, and measurement, so any change mixes causes. The rule's contribution can be separated only when the comparison is like for like.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed between the two years.

stimulus.body: A performance note states that the agency's target is to keep delay minutes below 1.2 per 100 train miles. options.misconception: Suspends the standard because of an unrelated project.

questions.explanation: Judging against a threshold means naming which measure is compared with which value: today meets the standard, the quarter does not. A mid-quarter upgrade is context, not grounds for dropping the standard.

questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to report results that fall short of a stated standard
questions.stem: A standard is set at 95 percent on-time departures. A new timetable gives 93 percent on the tested corridor and 94 percent on the untested one. Explain how the board should judge this.

answer.exemplar: Both figures fall below the 95 percent standard, so on the evidence given the timetable has not met the requirement and the board should say so plainly. The two figures should also be reported together, since 93 and 94 percent are close and the gap between them tells the board nothing about whether either reaches the standard. If the board wants to judge improvement as well as attainment, it needs the pre-change baseline for the same corridors before any judgement is made.

questions.explanation: The standard is a threshold for attainment and both corridors fall short, so the requirement is not met. Comparing the two new figures with each other says nothing about attainment.
questions.hint: Ask whether each figure clears the bar on its own.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an incomplete search on a review's conclusion
questions.stem: A second reviewer finds that the review excluded a 2018 study reporting no benefit, because it was published in a journal the team did not index. Explain the effect this has on the review's conclusion.

answer.exemplar: The review's conclusion rests on a literature search that was never complete, so the absence of contrary evidence is an artefact of which journals were indexed rather than a finding about the evidence. A review should state its databases, search terms, and inclusion criteria in advance and record every eligible excluded study with a reason tied to those criteria. Where the search was incomplete, the honest conclusion is that the question remains unsettled, not that benefits are established.

questions.explanation: An incomplete search cannot support a claim that the evidence favours an intervention, since missing studies are often missing because of their results. The honest conclusion is that the question is unsettled.
questions.hint: Ask why that particular journal was missing studies.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a threshold needs a stated statistic before it can be applied
questions.stem: A policy sets a maximum of 5 minutes of delay per 100 train miles for any single train. Explain why judging each train against that number needs care.

answer.exemplar: A per-train maximum applied to every train means the measure is heavily skewed by a small number of badly delayed trains, so the headline number can look acceptable while a large share of passengers experience long waits. The policy should state whether the limit is a mean, a median, or a percentile, whether it is averaged across services or per train, and how multi-day delays are counted. Those choices decide what the number means.

questions.explanation: Delay distributions are skewed, so the same threshold describes very different experiences depending on the statistic chosen. The policy must name the statistic, the averaging level, and how repeats are treated.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of average the policy means.

answer.exemplar: The debriefing must tell the crews that the monitoring described was a research design rather than a real disciplinary process, correct the fear it created, and give them the option to withdraw any statements they made under it. questions.explanation: The deception created a false belief with consequences for participants, so the debriefing must remove it and restore their choice. Leaving it in place lets the harms continue after data collection ends.

answer.exemplar: The claim bundles an unknown set of studies behind a single number and a vague count, so no reader can judge what the studies measured, on which networks, or whether they really agreed. 1) Apply to all data 2) Define rules 3) Report the count 4) Repeat with and without
options.misconception: Applies exclusions before defining them.

options.text: 1) Define rules 2) Report the count 3) Apply to all data 4) Repeat with and without
options.misconception: Reports the count before filtering.

options.text: 1) Define rules 2) Apply to all data 3) Repeat with and without 4) Report the count
options.misconception: Reports the count after the sensitivity check.

questions.explanation: Exclusions are defined, applied without reference to the outcome, then counted and tested for their influence. Two of these orders apply rules before defining them or report influence after the fact.
questions.hint: The rule comes before the data are filtered.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Attribute an improvement cautiously when other changes occurred

stimulus.body: A comparison note records that before the rule, delay minutes per 100 miles were 1.60 on the upgraded corridor and 1.45 on the comparison corridor. After the rule they are 1.10 and 1.42. The note also records that the upgraded corridor received two extra rescue locomotives during the same period.

questions.stem: Given the note, how should the board read the improvement on the upgraded corridor?

options.text: The corridor improved more than the comparison, but the extra locomotives mean the rule's contribution cannot be isolated.
The rule produced the full improvement, since the comparison corridor barely moved over the same period.
options.misconception: Assigns the whole change to the rule.

options.text: The comparison proves the rule works, because a corridor with help still improved while the other did not.
options.misconception: Misreads the comparison as isolating the rule.

options.text: The figures should not be reported, since they show the rule has no benefit.
options.misconception: Overstates what the figures reveal about the rule.

questions.explanation: The gap between corridors grew, which is the pattern a real effect would produce, but the rescue locomotives changed at the same time as the rule. Because two things moved together, the figures cannot separate them.
questions.hint: Count the changes that moved together.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify what still needs checking after a well-received debriefing
questions.stem: A debriefing session ends and 90 percent of crews leave saying they understood. What still needs checking before the study is written up as successful?

options.text: Whether the debriefing reached everyone, and whether the false belief was corrected rather than merely explained.
Whether the session ran long enough to satisfy the training requirement of 90 minutes.
options.misconception: Replaces the ethical question with a duration rule.

options.text: Whether the crews enjoyed the session, since satisfaction predicts debriefing quality.
options.misconception: Uses satisfaction as a proxy for correction.

options.text: Whether the payment was made on time, since prompt payment improves debriefing participation.
options.misconception: Links debriefing quality to administrative factors.

questions.explanation: Positive impressions from those who attended say little about non-attendees or about whether the false belief was actually replaced. The write-up must address coverage and correction, not satisfaction.
questions.hint: Ask who was not in the room, and what they still believe.
